notes: \cpara{Sums up the author's earlier posts on rationalization, with a link on each word. The claim that beating this ``metabias'' would let us ``recover from almost any other error of fact'' is given without argument.}
\cpara{States the problem for decisions: seeing what a criterion really endorses. The figures agree: \$1 million buys 5,000 laptops at \$200 each.}
\cpara{Says, with ``seem,'' that people can argue any goal into any action, and gives two rhetorical examples.}

\clogic{The knack was hedged with ``seem'' a sentence earlier; its evolutionary explanation is not hedged at all (``There's no mystery about this''), and no evidence is given for it. The Uglak line is a joke.}
\cpara{Asks how anyone could prove what a goal implies, using Mugabe as the example; the post itself calls the obvious answer ``a good guess.''}

\cpara{Asks whether rationalization can even be proved without a known criterion, and answers yes in a parenthesis: people's views on office politics track their interests. So what the post needs a pure optimizer for is not proof that rationalization happens, but knowing exactly what a criterion implies. The next paragraph asks for that.}
\cpara{Asks for an optimizer with a known goal and no other desires, whose output can be compared with human rationalizations of that goal.}
\cpara{Answers: natural selection, which has no human sympathies and optimizes only inclusive genetic fitness, though it does not maximize it.}
\cpara{Gives the comparison: the group selectionists predicted restraint; the laboratory produced cannibalism. On the four traits Wade reported, see the notes on the previous post.}

\cfact{I found no prediction by Wynne-Edwards about selection for small population size; Wade's experiment came fourteen years after his book. His hypothesis concerned social conventions that keep numbers below what the food will bear, with surplus animals dying (see the notes on ``The Tragedy of Group Selectionism'').}
\cpara{Raises the objection that human morality does not care about genetic fitness.}

\cpara{Answers by analogy: learn to hear a single note before an orchestra. No evidence is given that practice on evolutionary cases improves the judgement of moral principles. In the post's own example the answer came from a laboratory result, and the post's premise is that for human criteria no such check exists.}
